title: The Duchess of Malfi
author: John Webster
setting: Amalfi, Rome, Loreto, Ancona and Milan in the first years of the sixteenth century; the horoscope Bosola picks up is dated 1504
lengthNote: Five acts and roughly 25,000 words, longer than Macbeth and shorter than Hamlet; the last act runs for five scenes after the title character has died
openingLine: You are welcome to your country, dear Antonio; You have been long in France, and you return A very formal Frenchman in your habit: How do you like the French court?
summary: A young widowed duchess, told by her two brothers never to marry again, proposes to her steward and marries him in her own chamber with her maid hidden behind the arras as witness. The brothers have already planted a spy in her household. The secret holds for years and three children, until a dropped horoscope and a false key bring Ferdinand to her bedside. What follows is imprisonment staged as theatre, a strangling, and a revenge by the spy who did the work, in which every blow lands on the wrong person or too late.
referenceStyle: act.scene, following the divisions of the source text, which prints no line numbers and divides Act 1 into three scenes

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The Duchess of Malfi, in an early twentieth-century modernised edition
sourceText.note: The file is Webster's play as printed in 1623, with spelling partly modernised, editorial additions in square brackets and numbered footnotes, which are left out of the quotations. It keeps older forms such as 'apricocks' and sets contractions with a space ('She 's', 'I 'll'), and quotations follow it exactly. Act 1 falls into three scenes here, so the wooing is 1.3; editions that print Act 1 as one or two scenes number it differently. There are no line numbers, so references stop at the scene.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: After 1610, since the Cardinal mentions Galileo's telescope; before December 1614, when William Ostler, the first Antonio, died.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: A quarto printed by Nicholas Okes for John Waterson, the year of Shakespeare's First Folio, with a list of the King's Men who had acted it.

atAGlance.label: Playhouses
atAGlance.note: The title page names both: the company's candlelit indoor theatre in the city and its open-air house on Bankside.

atAGlance.label: A true story
atAGlance.note: A duchess of Amalfi who secretly married her steward, Antonio Beccadelli di Bologna, and vanished with her children; Antonio was later killed in Milan.

atAGlance.label: Source
atAGlance.note: Webster followed William Painter's English version in The Palace of Pleasure, itself taken from a French adaptation of Matteo Bandello's Italian novella.

atAGlance.label: First Bosola
atAGlance.note: The 1623 cast list gives Ferdinand to Richard Burbage and later Joseph Taylor, and the Duchess to a boy actor, Richard Sharpe.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A marriage made in private
structure.summary: Antonio, back from France, compares a well-run court to a fountain and then sketches the three siblings for Delio. The brothers take on Bosola as their spy, under cover of a post in their sister's stables, and warn her in a duet that sounds rehearsed never to marry again. Within minutes of their leaving she proposes to Antonio, puts her ring on his finger and marries him before a hidden witness.

scenes.title: The court-gall
scenes.summary: Antonio praises the French king's reformed court; Bosola, lately out of the galleys, rails at the Cardinal who will not reward him.

scenes.title: Portraits and a hiring
scenes.summary: Antonio describes Ferdinand, the Cardinal and the Duchess; Ferdinand buys Bosola as an intelligencer with gold and the provisorship of the horse.

scenes.title: The will and the ring
scenes.summary: The brothers forbid remarriage; the Duchess woos Antonio while dictating her will and marries him by spoken contract, Cariola listening behind the arras.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A birth that cannot be hidden
structure.summary: Time has passed and the Duchess is heavily pregnant. Bosola tests her with early apricots; she goes into labour, and Antonio locks the court into its chambers on the pretext of stolen jewels. Bosola picks up the horoscope Antonio has cast for the child and writes to Rome, where the Cardinal is entertaining his mistress and Ferdinand arrives with the letter, raving.

scenes.title: The apricots
scenes.summary: Bosola mocks an old lady's cosmetics, meditates on the rotten body and gives the Duchess apricots; she falls into labour.

scenes.title: The locked court
scenes.summary: Antonio has the gates shut and the officers confined; Cariola brings news of a son.

scenes.title: The dropped paper
scenes.summary: Bosola and Antonio meet at night with lantern and sword; Antonio's nose bleeds on his initials and he drops the child's nativity.

scenes.title: The Cardinal and Julia
scenes.summary: In Rome the Cardinal lectures his mistress on women's inconstancy; Delio offers her gold.

scenes.title: The letter
scenes.summary: Ferdinand rages at his sister in images of burning and butchery while the Cardinal tells him to control himself.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Discovery, a noble lie and banishment
structure.summary: Years later there are three children and the rumour is loose. Ferdinand comes into the bedchamber with a key Bosola has had made, hears his sister talking to a husband who has left the room, hands her a dagger and goes. She sends Antonio away under a pretended charge of false accounts, then tells Bosola the truth because he has praised Antonio so warmly. At Loretto the Cardinal exchanges his hat for a soldier's sword and has the family banished; Bosola returns in a visor to take the Duchess home as a prisoner.

scenes.title: The quiet brother
scenes.summary: Antonio tells Delio the court thinks him a thief; Ferdinand assures the Duchess he will believe no rumours.

scenes.title: The bedchamber
scenes.summary: Ferdinand overhears the Duchess and gives her a poniard; she dismisses Antonio as a bad steward, then confides in Bosola.

scenes.title: Soldiers and brothers
scenes.summary: In Rome the Cardinal is made a general; Bosola reports and Ferdinand learns that the husband is Antonio.

scenes.title: Loretto
scenes.summary: In a dumb show the Cardinal lays down his hat and robes and has the family banished while churchmen sing; two pilgrims ask by what justice.

scenes.title: The fisher's basket
scenes.summary: The Duchess sends Antonio and their eldest son towards Milan and is taken by Bosola's guard, answering him with a fable.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Despair by design
structure.summary: Ferdinand sets out to drive his sister to despair before he kills her. In the dark he gives her a dead man's hand wearing her ring and shows her wax figures of her husband and children as corpses; he sends madmen to sing and dance at her door; Bosola comes disguised as an old tomb-maker, then as the bellman. She is strangled with Cariola and two of the children. Ferdinand looks at her face and begins to go mad; Bosola, refused his reward, sees her revive for one word and die.

scenes.title: The dead hand
scenes.summary: The Duchess kisses a severed hand in the dark and is shown the wax figures; Bosola begins to refuse the work.

scenes.title: The tomb-maker
scenes.summary: Madmen, a dirge and the cords; Ferdinand's 'Cover her face', his denial of his own orders, and Bosola's change of heart over her body.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Revenge in the dark
structure.summary: In Milan Antonio resolves to visit the Cardinal at midnight and seek a reconciliation. Ferdinand, convinced he is a wolf, attacks his doctor. The Cardinal hires Bosola to kill Antonio and poisons Julia with a kissed Bible when she learns his secret. Bosola, meaning to protect Antonio, kills him by mistake in the dark, then stabs the Cardinal, whose cries go unanswered because he told his courtiers he would only be pretending. Ferdinand and Bosola wound each other, and Delio brings in the Duchess's son.

scenes.title: Nets to entrap you
scenes.summary: Pescara refuses Antonio's confiscated land to Delio and gives it to Julia, as fit payment for an injustice.

scenes.title: Lycanthropia
scenes.summary: Ferdinand tries to throttle his shadow; the Cardinal hires Bosola, and Julia dies of the poisoned book.

scenes.title: The echo
scenes.summary: By the ruins under the Cardinal's window an echo gives Antonio's words back to him as warnings.

scenes.title: The wrong man
scenes.summary: The Cardinal forbids anyone to answer cries in the night; Bosola, expecting an assassin, stabs Antonio.

scenes.title: A kind of nothing
scenes.summary: Bosola kills the Cardinal, Ferdinand and Bosola wound each other, and Delio presents the heir.

characters.name: The Duchess of Malfi
characters.role: A young widow who holds the dukedom of Amalfi as dowager
characters.summary: She is never given a first name. She is quick, funny and used to command, and she courts Antonio the way she would conduct business, by dictating to him. What her brothers call lust she treats as ordinary life: a husband, children, hair beginning to grey. In prison she is stripped of everything rank gave her, and speaks with more authority than at any point before.
characters.clue: She proposes to a man while pretending to make her will.
traits: proud of her rank to the end

relationships.label: trusts with her secret, and is betrayed by

characters.name: Antonio Bologna
characters.role: Steward, or great-master, of the Duchess's household; her second husband
characters.summary: The best judge of other people in the play and the least able to act on his judgement. He opens with a speech on how a court should be ordered and wins the tilting at the ring, but once married he is always a step behind: he drops the horoscope, flees when told to, and walks into the dark in the last act hoping to talk the Cardinal into kindness. His virtue is real and his birth is low, and the question of which counts runs through the play.
characters.clue: A gentleman of the household who marries its mistress, then spends the play being sent away from it.

relationships.label: suspects, and is killed by in error
a fellow servant who kept his honesty
relationships.note: Both are gentlemen of small means employed by the great. One is praised for his worth and ruined for it; the other is paid for his usefulness and ruined by that.

relationships.label: goes by night to seek reconciliation with

characters.name: Daniel de Bosola
characters.role: Provisor of the horse to the Duchess; her brothers' intelligencer
characters.summary: A scholar who served seven years in the galleys for a murder the Cardinal was thought to have commissioned, and came out unrewarded. He sees through everyone at court and says so in the play's sharpest prose, then takes Ferdinand's gold anyway. His contempt for the world is the malcontent's, but his conscience keeps working: he will not see the Duchess 'in mine own shape', weeps over her body, and spends the last act on a revenge in which he kills the man he meant to save.
characters.clue: He praises Antonio so well that the Duchess tells him her secret, and he reports it.

relationships.label: is hired as spy and executioner by
went to the galleys for, and is still unrewarded by
spies on, imprisons and has strangled
means to save, and kills by mistake

characters.name: Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria
characters.summary: He speaks of honour and the royal blood of Aragon, but his language about his sister comes back again and again to her body and what she does with it. He will not give a reason for forbidding her to marry, and when he does give one, over her corpse, it is money. He hires Bosola and devises the torments of Act IV, then denies he ordered anything. By Act V he believes he is a wolf with the hair on the inside.
characters.clue: Looking at her body, he says they were twins, and that if he died now he would have lived her time to a minute.

characters.name: The Cardinal
characters.role: Brother to Ferdinand and the Duchess; a prince of the church
characters.summary: Colder than Ferdinand and more dangerous for it. Antonio says he bribed his way towards the papacy and lays plots worse than any imposed on Hercules; Delio says he was thought to have commissioned the murder that sent Bosola to the galleys. He tells Ferdinand to calm down because the rage is noisy; he has no objection to it. He keeps a mistress, exchanges his hat for a general's sword in public ceremony, poisons Julia with a Bible, and dies asking to be laid by and never thought of.
characters.clue: He kills a woman by having her kiss a book.

characters.name: Cariola
characters.summary: Witness to the marriage, keeper of the secret and the one person the Duchess can talk to plainly. She thinks the match 'a fearful madness' and the feigned pilgrimage a jest with religion, and says so, but she stays. Her death is the counterweight to her mistress's: where the Duchess kneels, Cariola bites, scratches and claims to be with child to live a minute longer.
characters.clue: She hides behind the arras for the wedding.

relationships.label: serves and keeps the secret of
dies beside, in the opposite manner

characters.name: Julia
characters.role: Castruccio's wife and the Cardinal's mistress
characters.summary: She chooses her lovers as openly as the Duchess chooses in secret, and the play treats her with more comedy and less sympathy. She lies to her husband to reach Rome, fences with Delio over his gold, and in Act V holds a pistol on Bosola to declare that she loves him. Bosola uses her to draw out the Cardinal's secret, and the Cardinal kills her for knowing it.
characters.clue: She tells her old husband she has gone to Rome to visit an anchorite.
traits: expendable to the men who use her

relationships.label: a second woman who picks her own lover

characters.name: Delio
characters.summary: The man Antonio talks to, which makes him the audience's guide to the court in Act I. He is loyal, practical and a little worldly: he suggests the cover story of poisoned apricots, asks Pescara for Antonio's land to find out where it is going, and advises against the midnight visit. He is the only survivor with a speech, and he uses it to set the heir in his mother's place.
characters.clue: He speaks the play's last lines, about a footprint in snow.

relationships.label: is taught to ask noble things by

characters.name: The Marquis of Pescara
characters.role: A soldier, one of the Emperor's commanders in Italy
characters.summary: One of the few men of rank in the play who behaves as rank is supposed to. He refuses Delio a grant of Antonio's confiscated land because it was taken without course of law, and gives it instead to Julia as fit 'salary' for the Cardinal's lust. In the final scene he is the one courtier who goes down to answer the Cardinal's cries. He shows that greatness and goodness can meet in one man, which makes the other great men harder to excuse.
characters.clue: He will not give a friend what was stolen, but gives it to the Cardinal's mistress.

relationships.label: refuses to share in the injustice of

characters.name: The Madmen
characters.role: Inmates of the common hospital, sent to the Duchess's lodging
characters.summary: A mad lawyer, a secular priest, a doctor, an astrologer, an English tailor, a gentleman-usher, a farmer and a broker, let loose by Ferdinand to sing and dance at his sister's door. Their talk satirises the professions, from heraldry to law that eats to the bone, and the Duchess says that their noise is what keeps her sane. They are Ferdinand's cruelty turned into entertainment, and a forecast of his own madness in Act V.
characters.clue: The Duchess says she thanks her brother for them.

themes.name: Marriage and the widow's choice
themes.summary: The Duchess marries without a priest, a witness of rank or her family's leave, by a spoken contract she has heard lawyers call absolute marriage. In the wooing every ceremony takes on a private meaning: a will becomes a proposal, a ring a cure for a sore eye, a kneeling steward a man to be raised. Her brothers call remarriage lust. The play shows a household, three children and a woman who wanted an ordinary life and had to hide it.
themes.development: The brothers' warning and the wooing in 1.3; the domestic teasing of 3.2 that Ferdinand overhears; the dead man's hand wearing her wedding ring in 4.1.

themes.name: Rank and greatness
themes.summary: ‘The misery of us that are born great’ is the Duchess’s line, and the play looks at it from every side. Rank obliges her to propose, lets her brothers imprison her without trial, and decides who is paid and who hanged. Antonio's low birth is the whole charge against him. Images of height and falling run through the verse, from Bosola's crooked plum-trees to the pyramid that ends 'in a little point, a kind of nothing'.
themes.development: Greatness is a privilege in Act I, a prison in Act IV and, in Delio's last speech, a footprint in snow that melts when the sun comes out.

themes.name: Watching and being watched
themes.summary: The court runs on information. Bosola is hired as an intelligencer, reads the Duchess's body for signs of pregnancy, obtains a false key to her bedchamber and draws out her secret by praising her husband. Her defence is concealment of her own, a hidden witness, a pretended crime, a pretended pilgrimage, and the play is unsentimental about the cost: the woman who marries behind an arras has entered the same world of secrecy as her brothers.
themes.development: The arras in 1.3, the apricots in 2.1, the key and the eavesdropping in 3.2, and the darkness in which Ferdinand visits her in 4.1.

themes.name: Service, reward and the intelligencer
themes.summary: Nearly everyone below the three siblings is a servant looking for preferment. Bosola went unrewarded for his years in the galleys and is refused payment for the murders he commits; Antonio is dismissed as a bad steward and the officers who flattered him jeer as he goes; the Cardinal's courtiers promise to ignore his cries and keep their word. Webster shows service as a market in which loyalty is bought, and the servant is left holding the guilt.
themes.development: 'I am your creature' in 1.2; 'the inconstant And rotten ground of service' in 3.2; 'rather sought To appear a true servant than an honest man' in 4.2.

themes.name: Reputation, blood and fame
themes.summary: The brothers claim to act for the royal blood of Aragon and Castile, and Ferdinand's fable makes Reputation the one companion who, once lost, is never found again. The Duchess tells Cariola she has trusted her with 'More than my life,--my fame'. The play's own verdict comes last: great names melt like prints in snow, and only integrity of life survives its owner.
themes.development: From the Duchess's trust in Cariola in 1.3, through Ferdinand's fable in 3.2, to Delio's closing couplet in 5.5.

themes.name: Death and the body
themes.summary: Bosola sees the body as a box of worm-seed and a rotten corpse dressed in silk, and much of the play's imagery follows him into tombs, charnel-houses and graves. The Duchess faces the same facts differently. She calls death the best gift her brothers can give, kneels for it, and spends her last instructions on her son's cold. Her lines about death's ten thousand doors are the play's reply to Bosola's disgust.
themes.development: The alabaster figure she refuses to be in 1.3; the wax figures, the tomb-maker and the cords in Act IV; the echo from her grave in 5.3.

themes.name: Conscience
themes.summary: Conscience comes late in this play and mends nothing. Bosola argues with his before taking the job, obeys it only after the murder, and finds a guilty conscience 'a perspective That shows us hell'. Ferdinand's breaks out as madness at the sight of his sister's face. The Cardinal, who never seems troubled, spends his last scene alone with a book about hell, seeing a figure with a rake in his fish-ponds.
themes.development: Bosola's asides in 1.2; his refusal to appear in his own shape in 4.1; his tears over the body in 4.2; the Cardinal's 'How tedious is a guilty conscience!' in 5.5.

techniques.name: Prose against verse
techniques.definition: Moving between prose and verse to mark a change of rank, mood or purpose.
techniques.inThisBook: Bosola rails in prose and turns to verse when he moves from satire to meditation or to business, sometimes within one speech: 'Observe my meditation now' in 2.1 is the hinge. His prison speeches to the Duchess are prose, and her answer, 'I am Duchess of Malfi still', drops into them as a plain sentence that the verse around it cannot improve.

techniques.name: Sententiae
techniques.definition: A moral maxim, often a rhyming couplet, that draws a general truth from a particular event.
techniques.inThisBook: Webster closes scenes and speeches with rhymed sayings in the old style: 'She 's oft found witty, but is never wise'; 'There 's no deep valley but near some great hill'; 'Like diamonds, we are cut with our own dust'. They sound settled and rarely are. Many come from the people least entitled to moralise, and the gap between the maxim and the speaker's conduct is part of the effect.

techniques.name: Animal imagery
techniques.definition: Comparisons of people with beasts, measuring how far they have fallen from being human.
techniques.inThisBook: The brothers see their sister as a hyena and a screech-owl and her children as cubs and young wolves; she sees herself as a caged bird and, in her fable, a salmon. The imagery ends by becoming literal, when Ferdinand is met at midnight in a lane behind a church with a man's leg on his shoulder, claiming to be a wolf.

techniques.name: Stage property
techniques.definition: An object handled on stage that carries far more weight than its use in the scene explains.
techniques.inThisBook: Webster's properties are bodies and parts of bodies: apricots eaten greedily as proof of pregnancy, a poniard handed over as advice, a dead man's hand wearing a wedding ring, wax figures of a family, and a coffin, cords and bell brought as a 'present'. The Cardinal's poisoned Bible is the last of them, a holy object turned into a weapon.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows what a character on stage does not, so the words mean more than the speaker intends.
techniques.inThisBook: The Duchess speaks her most intimate lines to a husband who has left the room and a brother who has come into it. The Cardinal warns his courtiers that he may feign cries for help, and dies calling for help that his courtiers take for play-acting. Ferdinand’s quip that such weddings are more like executions than celebrations turns out to be a plan.

techniques.name: The political fable
techniques.definition: A short beast-story or allegory told inside the play to make an argument about power and worth.
techniques.inThisBook: Twice a character stops the action to tell a story. Ferdinand's fable of Reputation, Love and Death tells his sister she has lost the one companion who cannot be recovered; her fable of the salmon and the dog-fish answers Bosola's sneer at Antonio's birth by pointing out that no fish is valued until it is dead. Both are about worth and who gets to fix it.

techniques.name: The malcontent
techniques.definition: A stock figure of Jacobean drama: a disappointed, usually poor and educated man who rails at the corruption of the court he is trying to rise in.
techniques.inThisBook: Bosola is the type with its contradictions left in. Antonio sees straight away that he rails at what he wants, and Ferdinand tells him to keep his ‘old garb of melancholy’ as cover. The railing is accurate, which makes him the play's best satirist, and it changes nothing about what he will do for money until Act IV.

quotations.text: He and his brother are like plum-trees that grow crooked over standing-pools; they are rich and o'erladen with fruit, but none but crows, pies, and caterpillars feed on them.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: The Cardinal has just brushed Bosola off, though Bosola went to the galleys in his service.
quotations.analysis: The image condemns the brothers and the man who wants to feed on them in the same sentence. The trees are rich but crooked, rooted in stagnant water, and only scavengers profit, among whom Bosola immediately counts himself: he would hang on their ears like a horseleech ‘till I were full’. The malcontent's contempt and his appetite are one impulse.

quotations.text: Say, then, my corruption Grew out of horse-dung: I am your creature.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Ferdinand has offered Bosola gold to spy on the Duchess, then tells him he has also got him a post in her stables.
quotations.analysis: Bosola has just refused the gold as devils' wages, and he takes the job anyway. The bitter joke about horse-dung looks forward to the apricots ripened in the same stuff in Act II. A 'creature' was a dependant made by a patron's favour, and also a thing created: the word hands Ferdinand ownership of whatever Bosola is about to become.

quotations.text: Such weddings may more properly be said To be executed than celebrated.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Ferdinand and the Cardinal warn their sister against a secret remarriage.
quotations.analysis: In the pun a wedding is a death sentence, and it is spoken before any wedding has taken place. It sounds like a courtier's quip, but Ferdinand is the one person in a position to make it literally true, and he does. The brothers share their warning so smoothly between them that the Duchess remarks the speech must have been 'studied'.

quotations.text: For I am going into a wilderness, Where I shall find nor path nor friendly clue To be my guide.
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Her brothers gone, the Duchess sends Cariola behind the arras and waits for Antonio.
quotations.analysis: A moment earlier she said she would make her royal kindred her 'low footsteps'; now the confidence gives way to a clear sight of the danger. A 'clue' was a ball of thread, the kind Ariadne gave Theseus for the labyrinth, so the image admits that nobody has marked a way through what she is about to do. She goes in regardless, and that is the play's first definition of her courage.

quotations.text: The misery of us that are born great! We are forc'd to woo, because none dare woo us; And as a tyrant doubles with his words, And fearfully equivocates, so we Are forc'd to express our violent passions In riddles and in dreams
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Antonio has kept misreading her hints, and the Duchess stops hinting.
quotations.analysis: Rank reverses the order of courtship, and she sees the cost precisely: she must do the wooing, and do it in riddles. Comparing herself to a tyrant who equivocates is startling in a love scene and exact about her position, since she can marry only by using the authority that makes marriage impossible. 'Violent passions' is exactly what her brothers will accuse her of.

quotations.text: This is flesh and blood, sir; 'Tis not the figure cut in alabaster Kneels at my husband's tomb.
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Antonio kneels, trembling, and the Duchess raises him.
quotations.analysis: The widow of convention is a stone figure kneeling on her husband's tomb for ever, and the Duchess refuses the part in so many words. The line sets living flesh against carved stone, and Act IV reverses it with deliberate cruelty: she is shown wax figures of her family, Cariola tells her she looks like 'some reverend monument', and Bosola comes to make her tomb.

quotations.text: Whether the spirit of greatness or of woman Reign most in her, I know not; but it shows A fearful madness.
quotations.speaker: Cariola
quotations.context: The last lines of Act I, spoken alone after the couple have gone to bed.
quotations.analysis: The only witness to the marriage is also its first critic. Cariola cannot tell whether the pride of a prince or the desire of a woman is driving her mistress, and she leaves the question with the audience. 'Fearful' means both frightening and full of fear, and the pity she offers in her next breath reads as a forecast.

quotations.text: Though we are eaten up of lice and worms, And though continually we bear about us A rotten and dead body, we delight To hide it in rich tissue
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: After mocking an old lady's cosmetics in prose, Bosola announces 'my meditation' and turns to verse.
quotations.analysis: The speech moves from prose to verse as it moves from satire to sermon, and its subject is the body under the silk. The sentiment is the old contempt of the world, but Bosola is about to spend the scene inspecting a pregnant woman for evidence, and the disgust he voices is also the professional stance of a man paid to treat bodies as information.

quotations.text: I have a trick may chance discover it, A pretty one; I have bought some apricocks, The first our spring yields.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Bosola has listed the signs that the Duchess is pregnant: sickness, swelling, a loose gown.
quotations.analysis: He tests a theory with bait. The first apricots of the year, which he later tells her were ripened in horse-dung, become a pregnancy test, and her greed for them is taken as proof. The scene is comic in performance and invasive in substance: a woman's body is read without her consent, and the fruit brings on the labour it was meant to detect.

quotations.text: Though lust do mask in ne'er so strange disguise, She 's oft found witty, but is never wise.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Bosola has read the child's horoscope and means to send the news to Rome.
quotations.analysis: The couplet closes the scene like a moral, and it is spoken by a spy pleased with his own cleverness. 'Witty' meant ingenious: the Duchess is quick enough to hide the birth and not careful enough to hide the paper. Bosola can imagine her marriage only as lust in disguise, which is her brothers' reading before they have heard a word.

quotations.text: Methinks I see her laughing,-- Excellent hyena! Talk to me somewhat quickly, Or my imagination will carry me To see her in the shameful act of sin.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: In Rome, with Bosola's letter in his hand, Ferdinand raves to the Cardinal.
quotations.analysis: He asks to be distracted from a picture he cannot stop painting, and then paints it: a strong-thighed bargeman, a labourer from the wood-yard, a squire carrying coals. The hyena, believed to laugh and to feed on the dead, makes his sister a beast. The Cardinal's dry 'With whom?' shows how little the other brother shares this particular obsession.

quotations.text: For know, whether I am doom'd to live or die, I can do both like a prince.
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Brushing her hair, the Duchess talks to Antonio, not knowing that he has slipped out and Ferdinand has come in.
quotations.analysis: The boast is made to an empty room and answered by the wrong man, with a dagger and 'Die, then, quickly!' Before it she has joked about her brothers, her greying hair and more children; she ends on her rank, which is where Ferdinand strikes. That she can in fact do both like a prince is what Act IV sets out to prove.

quotations.text: 'Stay,' quoth Reputation, 'Do not forsake me; for it is my nature, If once I part from any man I meet, I am never found again.' And so for you: You have shook hands with Reputation, And made him invisible.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Ferdinand tells his sister what she has lost by marrying.
quotations.analysis: Love can be found among shepherds and Death in battles, but Reputation, once parted from, is gone for good. The formal fable, in the middle of a violent scene, shows what Ferdinand believes he is defending, and it is a thing that exists only in other people's opinion. The Duchess answers by asking why she alone, of all the princes of the world, should be 'cas'd up, like a holy relic'.

quotations.text: A politician is the devil's quilted anvil; He fashions all sins on him, and the blows Are never heard
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Alone, having just been told the secret, Bosola prepares to carry it to Ferdinand.
quotations.analysis: The 'politician', the stage schemer, is an anvil padded so that no hammer-blow is heard: every sin is shaped on him in silence. Bosola is describing himself as he goes to betray a woman who has just trusted him, and the next lines call his trade a 'base quality'. He sees his corruption exactly and continues with it.

quotations.text: The birds that live i' th' field On the wild benefit of nature live Happier than we; for they may choose their mates, And carol their sweet pleasures to the spring.
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Banished from Ancona, with most of her household gone, the Duchess tells Antonio of a dream in which her diamonds turned to pearls.
quotations.analysis: The comparison removes rank altogether. Birds choose their mates without asking anyone and sing about it in the open, the two freedoms her greatness has denied her. The image looks forward to her prison, where she will tell Cariola that the robin and the nightingale 'Never live long in cages'.

quotations.text: Our value never can be truly known, Till in the fisher's basket we be shown: I' th' market then my price may be the higher, Even when I am nearest to the cook and fire.
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Arrested by Bosola, who sneers at Antonio as 'One of no birth', the Duchess answers with a fable.
quotations.analysis: A dog-fish has rebuked a salmon for mixing with its betters; the salmon replies that both have escaped the same net, and that value is only known in the fisher's basket. It is her answer to rank: worth is fixed at death, not at birth, and the great are valued highest 'when they're most wretched'. She is describing her own case, and the next act bears her out.

quotations.text: Didst thou ever see a lark in a cage? Such is the soul in the body: this world is like her little turf of grass, and the heaven o'er our heads like her looking-glass, only gives us a miserable knowledge of the small compass of our prison.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Bosola comes to the Duchess's prison disguised as an old man, and she asks him who she is.
quotations.analysis: The soul is a caged lark and the sky a looking-glass that shows only how small the cage is. The image is traditional and the application is exact, since he is speaking to a woman imprisoned in her own palace. His purpose, he says later, is to bring her ‘By degrees to mortification’, and what he offers her is the argument that nothing she is losing was worth having; there is no comfort in it.

quotations.text: I am Duchess of Malfi still.
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Bosola has told her she must be 'some great woman, sure', since care has greyed her early and she sleeps worse than a mouse in a cat's ear.
quotations.analysis: Six words against everything Bosola has said about the body. 'Still' means both 'even now' and 'always', and it also suggests quiet, the composure she keeps against the noise of the madmen. She claims the title her brothers say she has forfeited, and Bosola answers that her rank is exactly what breaks her sleep. The scene lets both be true.

quotations.text: I know death hath ten thousand several doors For men to take their exits; and 'tis found They go on such strange geometrical hinges, You may open them both ways
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Bosola asks whether the manner of her death, the cord, does not terrify her.
quotations.analysis: She answers terror with geometry. Death is a building with countless exits, hinged both ways, and the method matters no more than which way a door swings. 'Exits' is a theatre word as well. The wit is the point: a woman about to be strangled will not let her killers set the tone, and asks only to be out of their ‘whispering’.

quotations.text: Cover her face; mine eyes dazzle: she died young.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Bosola shows Ferdinand the Duchess's body and asks, 'Do you not weep?'
quotations.analysis: Nine words in three clauses, none of them about what he feels. 'Dazzle' can mean blurred by tears or by too much light, and either way he cannot look. Then, for the first time, he gives reasons: they were twins, and he had hoped to gain 'An infinite mass of treasure by her death'. The line holds grief and guilt at the edge of speech.

quotations.text: I serv'd your tyranny, and rather strove To satisfy yourself than all the world: And though I loath'd the evil, yet I lov'd You that did counsel it; and rather sought To appear a true servant than an honest man.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Ferdinand has refused Bosola his reward and ordered him out of his sight.
quotations.analysis: The last line is the most exact self-judgement in the play. Bosola kept the act and the man who ordered it apart, loathing one and loving the other, and chose the look of loyalty over the fact of honesty. He says it to claim his pay; within a few lines, over the Duchess's body, he discovers that the distinction does not survive what it has done.

quotations.text: We are merely the stars' tennis-balls, struck and banded Which way please them.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Bosola has stabbed a man in the dark, expecting an assassin, and learns that it is Antonio.
quotations.analysis: The man who spent the play choosing his masters now blames the stars. 'Banded' is a tennis term, struck to and fro, and the image makes human life a game played by someone else. It is an evasion, and also, in an act made of accidents, a fair description of what keeps happening. The audience saw who was coming; Bosola did not.

quotations.text: In all our quest of greatness, Like wanton boys whose pastime is their care, We follow after bubbles blown in th' air.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Dying, Antonio learns that his wife and two of his children have been murdered.
quotations.analysis: His last philosophy is the play’s plainest statement of vanity. ‘Our quest of greatness’ takes in everyone, the brothers’ pride, Bosola’s hunt for preferment and his own rise by marriage, and the image of boys chasing bubbles makes the pursuit childish more than wicked. His final wish is that his son should 'fly the courts' of princes altogether.

quotations.text: I am puzzl'd in a question about hell; He says, in hell there 's one material fire, And yet it shall not burn all men alike. Lay him by. How tedious is a guilty conscience!
quotations.speaker: Cardinal
quotations.context: The Cardinal is alone with a book, waiting for Bosola to help him move Julia's body.
quotations.analysis: The most composed character in the play is reading theology and cannot keep his mind on it. His puzzle, one fire that burns each sinner differently, is a question about proportion and judgement, and he puts the book down to admit that conscience is tedious. Then he describes a figure with a rake in his fish-ponds. The guilt he never showed has been at work all along.

quotations.text: My sister, O my sister! there 's the cause on 't. Whether we fall by ambition, blood, or lust, Like diamonds, we are cut with our own dust.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Mortally wounded, Ferdinand recovers his wits for a moment.
quotations.analysis: His last words go back to the beginning. His sister is the cause, and the couplet generalises it: ambition, blood and lust, the Cardinal's, the family's and his own, destroy the great as diamonds are cut with their own powder. The Duchess compared a widow who remarries to a diamond in Act I; the image returns to judge the men who objected.

quotations.text: These wretched eminent things Leave no more fame behind 'em, than should one Fall in a frost, and leave his print in snow; As soon as the sun shines, it ever melts, Both form and matter.
quotations.speaker: Delio
quotations.context: Delio arrives with the Duchess's son to find the Cardinal, Ferdinand and Bosola dead.
quotations.analysis: The great leave no more trace than a body's print in snow, and 'form and matter' melt together. The image answers every character who killed to protect a name or a line, and the final couplet names what does last: 'Integrity of life is fame's best friend'. Delio says it while presenting an heir, though the play has mentioned a son from the Duchess's first marriage, which leaves the ending less settled than it sounds.

timeline.label: Giovanna d'Aragona widowed, c. 1498
timeline.detail: Her husband, Alfonso Piccolomini, Duke of Amalfi, died, and she governed the duchy for their son. Her brother Luigi was a cardinal.

timeline.label: The play's own date: Bosola's horoscope reads 1504
timeline.detail: The nativity Bosola picks up in 2.3 is dated 1504, which places the action, loosely, in the first years of the sixteenth century.

timeline.label: Antonio Bologna killed in Milan, c. 1513
timeline.detail: The historical Antonio Beccadelli di Bologna was murdered after the Duchess and their children had disappeared. Bandello, who says he knew him, names the leader of the killers as Daniele da Bozolo, the source of Bosola's name.

timeline.label: Bandello's novellas printed
timeline.detail: The Duchess's story appears in the first part of Matteo Bandello's collection of tales, published at Lucca.

timeline.label: The Palace of Pleasure, second volume
timeline.detail: William Painter's English version of the story, taken from a French adaptation of Bandello, is the one Webster followed most closely.

timeline.label: John Webster born, c. 1580
timeline.detail: The son of a London coachmaker. Almost nothing is known of his life, and the date is an inference.

timeline.label: Galileo's telescope
timeline.detail: Galileo published his observations of the moon this year. The Cardinal's reference in 2.4 to 'that fantastic glass Invented by Galileo the Florentine' places the play after it.

timeline.label: Arbella Stuart's secret marriage
timeline.detail: A cousin of James I married William Seymour without the king's leave and was imprisoned; she died in the Tower in 1615. Her case has often been set beside the Duchess's.

timeline.label: The White Devil printed
timeline.detail: Webster's first surviving tragedy of his own, another Italian story centred on a defiant woman, came out after a winter performance that he blamed for its poor reception.

timeline.label: Performed by December, when William Ostler, the first Antonio, dies
timeline.detail: William Ostler, named as Antonio in the 1623 cast list, died in December 1614, so the play had been performed by then.

timeline.label: The first quarto
timeline.detail: Printed by Nicholas Okes for John Waterson, with commendatory verses and a list of actors that covers two different casts.

timeline.label: Ashcroft and Gielgud at the Haymarket
timeline.detail: A London revival with Peggy Ashcroft as the Duchess and John Gielgud as Ferdinand, in the last months of the Second World War.

timeline.label: Chosen to open the new Sam Wanamaker Playhouse
timeline.detail: The candlelit indoor theatre at Shakespeare's Globe, modelled on playhouses of the Blackfriars kind, opened its first season with this play.

places.name: Amalfi
places.note: Webster's 'Malfi', on the coast south of Naples. Act I, the first three scenes of Act II, 3.1 and 3.2, and all of Act IV take place in the Duchess's palace.

places.name: Rome
places.note: The Cardinal's city: his scene with Julia in 2.4, Ferdinand's rage in 2.5 and the council of war in 3.3.

places.name: Loreto
places.note: The shrine of Our Lady of Loretto, 'scarce seven leagues From fair Ancona', where the Duchess's feigned pilgrimage ends in the dumb show of banishment.

places.name: Ancona
places.note: The free city where Antonio takes refuge and whose state banishes the family at the Cardinal's request.

places.name: Milan
places.note: The setting of Act V, where the brothers and Antonio converge and the historical Antonio was killed.

places.name: Blackfriars Playhouse site, London
places.note: The King's Men's indoor theatre, lit by candles, named first on the 1623 title page. Candlelight could make the darkness of Act IV a real effect there.

places.name: The Globe, Bankside
places.note: The company's open-air playhouse, where the play was also acted. The candlelit Sam Wanamaker Playhouse, a short walk away beside the modern Globe, opened with it in 2014.

criticalViews.position: A tragedy of a woman's right to choose
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the Duchess is the moral centre of the play and its argument. She marries for love across a barrier of rank, runs a household that is happy by every sign the play gives, and is destroyed by brothers whose motives are greed, pride and something darker. Act IV transfers authority from the powerful to the powerless: stripped of everything, she speaks with a clarity nobody else achieves, while her murderers go mad or die in the dark.
criticalViews.counter: The play does not make her choice simple. Cariola calls it 'a fearful madness', secrecy draws her into lies and a feigned pilgrimage, and she trusts Bosola on the strength of flattery. An audience could admire her constancy and still think that a ruling widow who marries her steward in secret has neglected her son and her state, and the play leaves room for both judgements.

criticalViews.summary: A second view reads the play within the assumptions of its own time, in which a widow's remarriage was suspect and a prince's marriage to a servant disordered the hierarchy on which everything rested. The Duchess herself insists she has not tried 'to create Any new world or custom', which shows she knows she is testing one, and the catastrophe follows from the test. The story reached Webster through retellings that treated it as a cautionary tale about appetite and rank.
criticalViews.counter: Webster changes his sources exactly here. He gives the Duchess the best verse and the best death, makes Bosola, a hostile witness, praise Antonio's worth, and lets two pilgrims ask by what justice she is banished. A play meant as a warning against her would hardly make her persecutors a lycanthrope and a poisoner.

criticalViews.position: Great scenes in a broken structure
criticalViews.summary: A long-standing complaint is that Webster writes superb scenes and uneven plays. The dead man's hand, the wax figures and the dance of madmen are sensational effects, and once the heroine is dead the fifth act dissolves into accident: a revenge that kills the wrong man, a Cardinal undone by his own trick, a heap of bodies. On this view the play’s power lies in its lines and its fourth act, not in its design.
criticalViews.counter: The fifth act can be read as the point, not the flaw. It shows a world with the Duchess gone: an echo from her grave, the brothers destroyed by their own methods of secrecy and pretence, and Bosola's good intentions producing only 'Such a mistake as I have often seen In a play'. The horrors of Act IV, meanwhile, belong to Ferdinand, and the play presents them as his cruelty, not as thrills of its own.

essayQuestions.question: How does Webster present the Duchess's decision to marry Antonio?
plan: Set out what the brothers forbid in 1.3 and how they do it: the rehearsed double act, the father's poniard, Ferdinand's refusal to give a reason. The prohibition is shown before the choice.
Read the wooing closely. The will that becomes a proposal, the ring, the raising of the kneeling steward and 'The misery of us that are born great' show a woman using her authority to escape it.
Weigh the cost. The marriage needs an arras and a hidden witness, and later a pretended crime and a pretended pilgrimage; Cariola's closing speech in 1.3 puts the case against.
Use 3.2 to show the marriage from the inside, jokes about lodging, children and greying hair, so that the audience sees a happy household before Ferdinand's dagger.
Conclude on 4.2: 'I am Duchess of Malfi still' suggests that the choice did not cost her the identity her brothers say she forfeited.

essayQuestions.question: 'Bosola is the most interesting character in the play because he is the most divided.' Discuss.
plan: Begin with how others see him in 1.1 and 1.2: Antonio's judgement that he rails at what he wants, the Cardinal's care not to be seen with him, Ferdinand's gold.
Trace the double voice: satirical prose and asides against himself ('Thus the devil Candies all sins o'er') set beside the efficiency with which he spies and reports.
Show the turn in Act IV: 'Never in mine own shape', the disguises of tomb-maker and bellman, the refused pension and 'rather sought To appear a true servant than an honest man'.
Treat Act V as a test of the change: good intentions, a killing by mistake, and a dying claim that his quarrel was just.
Conclude by asking whether the division makes him tragic or merely late, since conscience in this play arrives after the damage is done.

essayQuestions.question: How does Webster use spectacle and staging in Act IV?
plan: Identify Ferdinand as the author of the act's effects: the darkness, the dead hand, the wax figures, the madmen, the coffin, cords and bell.
Consider the Duchess's response to each. She kisses the hand, wishes to be bound to the figures, thanks her brother for the madmen and chooses how she will kneel.
Think about the playhouse. At a candlelit indoor theatre such as the Blackfriars, darkness and sudden light could be real effects, not something the audience had to imagine.
Look at Bosola's roles as tomb-maker and bellman, and at his dirge as a performance within the performance.
Conclude that Webster frames spectacle as cruelty: the horrors are Ferdinand's, and the Duchess's plain speech is the play's answer to them.

essayQuestions.question: What is the dramatic purpose of the fifth act, after the Duchess has died?
plan: Acknowledge the objection that the heroine dies at the end of Act IV and the last act can seem a mechanical clearing of the stage.
Show how the Duchess remains present: the echo from her grave in 5.3, Bosola's sense that she haunts him, Ferdinand's dying 'My sister, O my sister!'

Examine the pattern of error: Antonio's hope of reconciliation, Bosola's mistaken blow, the Cardinal's real cries taken for pretended ones. The brothers are undone by their own methods of secrecy and pretence.
Consider Pescara and Delio as the counterweight, a man of rank who refuses to profit from injustice and a friend who sets the heir in his mother's right.
Conclude on Delio's snow image: the act shows how little of greatness survives, an argument the Duchess's death alone could not complete.

discussionQuestions: Ferdinand gives no reason for forbidding his sister to remarry until she is dead. What reasons does the play let you infer, and which does it want you to believe?
Is the secret marriage an act of courage or of recklessness? Does the play need it to be one or the other?
Bosola arranges the Duchess's death and then sets out to avenge it. Can one character be both the instrument and the conscience of a crime?
The Duchess tells a fable about fish and Ferdinand one about Reputation. What does each speaker's choice of story reveal?
The Cardinal dies partly because he told his courtiers to ignore his cries. Where else in the play does secrecy defeat the person who relies on it?
How would you stage the madmen in 4.2 for an audience today: as comedy, as horror, or as something else?

related.why: A phrase-by-phrase reading of the tomb-maker scene, in which Bosola prices the body at nothing and the Duchess answers in six words.
Another soul in trouble a generation earlier; the Cardinal alone with a book and a question about hell is Faustus's last scene in a colder key.
A court run by spies and eavesdroppers, a revenger who kills the wrong man behind an arras, and a survivor left to tell the story.
A servant who advances by insinuation, and a woman destroyed by what men imagine about her body.
Another play in which a man in authority treats a woman's chastity as his to dispose of, and a private marriage contract turns the plot.
Machiavelli's Italy in the same decade as the play's action, and the plain case for the policy that Webster's courtiers practise and his malcontent despises.
